promise: After this you can explain what a circuit breaker and its three states do, how deadlines and retries differ from a breaker, and what load shedding adds on the server side.

terms.definition: A program that answers requests from other programs.
A service that another service calls in order to do its own work.
How long a caller waits for an answer before giving up.

before.note: Read Rate Limiting first: it caps how much one client may send, while this topic covers what to do when a dependency is failing or a server has too much work. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: When a service calls another service and the call starts to fail or hang, the caller can make things worse by trying again and again. A circuit breaker is a guard around such a call. Microsoft's architecture guidance describes it as stopping an application from repeatedly trying an operation that is likely to fail, while still letting the application notice when the fault is resolved [[azure-circuit-breaker]].

The guidance describes it as a state machine with three states, named after the breaker in an electrical panel. While Closed, requests go through and the breaker counts recent failures. If they pass a threshold within a time period, it becomes Open and starts a timeout timer. While Open, requests fail immediately with an error. When the timer ends it becomes Half-Open, where a limited number of requests are let through: if they succeed the breaker closes and the failure counter resets, and if any fail it opens again and restarts the timer [[azure-circuit-breaker]]. The page says the Half-Open state helps stop a recovering service from being flooded with requests [[azure-circuit-breaker]].

The other side of the problem is a server that has too much work. HTTP has a status code for a server that cannot handle a request for now: 503 Service Unavailable, for a temporary overload or scheduled maintenance that will likely be alleviated after some delay. The server may add a Retry-After header to suggest how long to wait [[rfc9110]]. A breaker protects a caller from a failing dependency. Turning requests away with a 503 is one way a server protects itself, which the topic page calls load shedding.

terms.definition: A guard around a call that stops making it for a while after enough failures, so it fails at once instead of waiting.
The breaker's three states in Microsoft's description: requests flow and failures are counted, requests fail immediately, and a limited number of requests test whether the fault is fixed.
Returning an error at once instead of waiting for a call that is likely to fail.
The HTTP status code for a server that cannot handle a request for now because of a temporary overload or maintenance.
An HTTP header a server may send with a 503 to suggest how long a client should wait before retrying.

stages.name: How it works
body: A breaker is only one of three things around a call. First, how long to wait. gRPC calls this a deadline: a point in time after which the client is unwilling to wait for a response. Some APIs use a timeout instead, the longest a call may take, and a timeout becomes a deadline by adding it to the current time [[grpc-deadlines]]. gRPC does not set a deadline by default, so a client can wait effectively forever. Its guide says to always set a realistic one, starting from what you know about network latency and server processing time and checking it with load testing [[grpc-deadlines]].

A server gives up on a call once the client's deadline has passed, but the application has to stop any work it started [[grpc-deadlines]]. When a server calls another server, the deadline can be passed on as a timeout with the time already used taken off, so a chain of calls shares one budget [[grpc-deadlines]].

Second, whether to try again. A retry replaces a failed call with a new one. gRPC's guide says retries help applications get past temporary problems, and recommends knowing which failures are suitable to retry, using exponential backoff to space the attempts, limiting how many there are, and watching retry metrics [[grpc-retry]]. Retries are on by default, but there is no default retry policy: without one, only a few low-level failures are retried, and only when gRPC is certain the server never processed the call [[grpc-retry]].

Third, when to stop calling at all, which is the breaker's job. Microsoft's page says the circuit breaker pattern serves a different purpose from retries. They can be combined, with the retry logic stopping when the breaker reports that the fault is not transient [[azure-circuit-breaker]].

stages.name: Going deeper
body: Not everything called a circuit breaker is the state machine from Stage 1. In Envoy's documentation, circuit breaking means resource limits, not the Closed, Open, Half-Open state machine: caps on the number of connections to a cluster, of requests waiting for a connection, of requests outstanding, of retries active at once, and of connection pools. Each limit is tracked per upstream cluster and per priority, and when one overflows a counter goes up. The page says it is nearly always better to fail quickly and apply back pressure downstream [[envoy-circuit-breaking]].

Envoy enforces these limits at the network level, so each application need not code them, and they are fully distributed, not coordinated: threads share the limits, but because the implementation is eventually consistent, a race can let a limit be exceeded a little [[envoy-circuit-breaking]]. The page shows modest defaults, for example 1024 connections per cluster. That is what it shows on 2026-10-11 and it may change [[envoy-circuit-breaking]].

A fixed limit has to be chosen by hand. Envoy also has an adaptive concurrency filter that adjusts how many requests may be outstanding to a cluster, calculated from latency samples of completed requests compared with the expected latency [[envoy-adaptive-concurrency]]. Its gradient controller uses an ideal round-trip time that it measures periodically [[envoy-adaptive-concurrency]]. The page gives the filter no status label such as experimental or stable, so none is claimed here.

Google's chapter on handling overload, from its SRE book (2017, guidance, not a specification), describes two ideas that match the topic page's load shedding. One is criticality: each request carries one of four values, from the most critical to the most sheddable, and an overloaded task rejects lower criticalities sooner [[google-sre-overload]]. The other is client-side throttling: a client that sees a significant share of its recent requests rejected by the backend as out of quota starts rejecting some itself, using counts of its requests and the backend's accepts over the last two minutes [[google-sre-overload]].
On the topic page, the [Uber post](/topic/circuit-breakers#uber-cinnamon-load-shedder-2023) describes a shedder that ranks requests by priority. It never mentions circuit breakers.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: A breaker has costs. AWS's builders' library article says, as AWS's own view, that circuit breakers are widely promoted to limit the extra load retries create, but that they bring modal behaviour into a system that can be hard to test and can add significant time to recovery. AWS says it instead limits retries locally with a token bucket [[aws-timeouts-retries]]. That is AWS's view, not a general rule.

AWS also describes retries as selfish: when failures come from overload, they add load and can delay recovery. Its example is a stack where each of five layers retries three times, which it says multiplies the load on the database by 243 [[aws-timeouts-retries]]. AWS prefers backoff, jitter and retrying at a single point in the stack, again as its own practice [[aws-timeouts-retries]].
Hystrix, a well-known breaker library from Netflix, says in its own README that it is in maintenance mode and no longer in active development [[hystrix-readme]].

Istio shows how a mesh configures this. Its task puts connection limits and outlier detection in one DestinationRule and sets the limits to 1, so that its own test can trip them [[istio-circuit-breaking]]. In the run printed on its page, 17 of 20 calls with two concurrent connections returned 200 and 3 returned 503, and with three connections 11 of 30 returned 200 [[istio-circuit-breaking]]. Those numbers are Istio's sample output, and another run will differ.

Why a breaker's probes can mislead is on the topic page. Microsoft's page says Half-Open exists so a recovering service is not flooded [[azure-circuit-breaker]], and the [Zalando post](/topic/circuit-breakers#zalando-circuit-breaker-herd-2026) shows a breaker whose healthy probes closed it, after which the full load arrived at once.

misconceptions.myth: A circuit breaker is one mechanism with one meaning.
misconceptions.truth: Microsoft describes a state machine of Closed, Open and Half-Open [[azure-circuit-breaker]], while Envoy's circuit breaking means limits on connections, pending requests, requests and retries [[envoy-circuit-breaking]].

misconceptions.myth: Retrying a failed call is always safe and helps.
misconceptions.truth: AWS says retries add load, which can make an overload worse and delay recovery [[aws-timeouts-retries]], and gRPC's guide recommends limiting attempts and using backoff [[grpc-retry]].

misconceptions.myth: A call with no deadline will fail on its own sooner or later.
misconceptions.truth: gRPC does not set a deadline by default, so a client can wait effectively forever [[grpc-deadlines]].

misconceptions.myth: A 503 means a server is gone for good.
misconceptions.truth: HTTP defines 503 for a temporary overload or scheduled maintenance that will likely be alleviated after some delay [[rfc9110]].

tryIt.intro: These are read-only examples from Istio's circuit breaking task, because running them needs a Kubernetes cluster with Istio installed [[istio-circuit-breaking]]. The numbers in the rule are Istio's own example values, deliberately tiny so a small test trips them. The results are as printed on Istio's page, and another run will differ.

commands.command:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: httpbin
spec:
  host: httpbin
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      tcp:
        maxConnections: 1
      http:
        http1MaxPendingRequests: 1
        maxRequestsPerConnection: 1
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 1
      interval: 1s
      baseEjectionTime: 3m
      maxEjectionPercent: 100
commands.shows: The rule the task applies with kubectl: connection limits and outlier detection for the httpbin service. Istio's page applies it with a heredoc given to kubectl apply -f -.
commands.warning: Applying this rule changes the traffic policy for the httpbin service in a cluster. Run it only on a test cluster.

commands.command: kubectl exec "$FORTIO_POD" -c fortio -- /usr/bin/fortio load -c 2 -qps 0 -n 20 -loglevel Warning http://httpbin:8000/get
commands.shows: Sends 20 calls over two concurrent connections. Istio's page prints Code 200: 17 (85.0 %) and Code 503: 3 (15.0 %), and notes that the proxy allows some leeway.
commands.warning: This sends 20 test requests to the httpbin service in your cluster. Run it only on a test cluster.

commands.command: kubectl exec "$FORTIO_POD" -c fortio -- /usr/bin/fortio load -c 3 -qps 0 -n 30 -loglevel Warning http://httpbin:8000/get
commands.shows: Sends 30 calls over three concurrent connections. Istio's page prints Code 200: 11 (36.7 %) and Code 503: 19 (63.3 %).
commands.warning: This sends 30 test requests to the httpbin service in your cluster. Run it only on a test cluster.
